extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics and creative writers studying classical theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance drawn from Aristotle's Poetics (with commentary) about how poetic and dramatic works should imitate life, choose forms (verse, tune, dance), portray character, and select treatment (narrative vs dramatic). Useful for writers and critics applying classical poetics to composition and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis (Imitation) as fundamental
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative art reproduces psychic motion; art imitates actions, characters and life (mimesis) rather than merely reproducing external appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art reproduces the form of motion (e.g. psychic motion) rather than literal likenesses; imitation is the basis for classifying arts and their aims. Examples and philosophic references (Aristotle, Problems) underline that imitation gives cognitive and aesthetic pleasure. Anti-pattern: treating art as mere copying of surfaces without rendering underlying motions or causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music imitates emotions by form of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Music suggests mental states because the sound as a form of motion reproduces the psychic motion; rhythm and harmony portray emotions and moods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific proponents (Witasek) argue notes imitate the forms emotions take (e.g. anger = steady irregular swelling and sinking). Use rhythm/harmony intentionally to evoke particular moods. Anti-pattern: assuming association of moods with airs is purely fanciful without testing audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dance imitates primarily by rhythm (beat/time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancers’ measures simulate with the rhythm itself: the beating of time is necessary for a dance, and dance movements portray moral qualities, emotions and experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dance can portray hunting, war, fishing, rowing, animal life and labor; dance’s mimetic power lies in forms of actual motion. Wallacek’s view that dance’s rhythm disciplines performers is noted. Anti-pattern: seeing dance purely as display of graceful movement without mimetic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and harmony jointly portray moral qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: In music, rhythm and harmony together portray moral qualities (characters, emotions); forms of music correspond to certain motions and experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts (e.g. Lanes, Wiraszek) find imitation chiefly in forms of motion to which music corresponds. Use combinations of rhythm and harmony deliberately to suggest character or action. Scoring note: consider how convincingly music/sonic elements map to intended psychic motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothing of the imagination: dance, tune, verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts employ different 'clothing' for the imagination (dance, tune, verse). Lyric poetry typically takes the form of verse, but the 'restraining element' in lyric is the tune rather than metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose which clothing(s) to use for an imaginative effect; recognize that some forms (dithyrambic, nomic, tragedy) may employ them simultaneously while others use them in different parts. Anti-pattern: misattributing the primary restraining force (metre vs tune).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre is not identical to poetry; metre is superimposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre is a variety of rhythm superimposed on language; metrical form is not the sole or essential feature of poetry (language and tune also matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that metre alone makes something poetry—consider the aim (art vs science) and the role of language/tune. Historical note: debate whether metre is distinctive of poetry. Anti-pattern: equating 'poet' solely with metrical composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative vs Dramatic (treatment) — past narration vs present realization
rubrics_metrics.description: A key distinction is treatment: the same fiction can be presented as narrative (telling of past events) or as drama (realization in the present); drama is realization, not imitation of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose treatment according to whether you want the audience to experience events as happening now (dramatic/enacted) or as recounted (narrative). Note: drama requires energeia (realization) and social interaction among characters. Anti-pattern: confusing direct speech forms with the deeper treatment distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy and Comedy defined by moral relative standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy portrays beings superior to ourselves; comedy portrays beings inferior to modern man — classification depends on relative moral quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing in these genres, select characters whose moral status (better, worse, or on a level with us) aligns with the genre’s aims. Example: tragedy often portrays heroes; comedy often portrays ignoble or low characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters are classificatory by moral quality (virtue/vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who portray persons must portray characters who are relatively good or bad; the differentia of character is virtue (or vice) and characters can be ranged on a scale of virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters with discernible moral qualities so that their differences are meaningful; physical externals may correspond to character (physiognomy). Anti-pattern: creating characters without clear moral differentiators or inconsistent moral types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist chooses types suited to temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist selects the type of subject and character that suits his individual temperament; the choice of type influences mode and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be self-aware about which kinds of characters or actions your temperament inclines you to portray; this choice should inform form and style. Example: some authors favor lampoons and satire, others heroic actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of reproduction — leave room for imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much reproduction (excessive detail) diminishes aesthetic pleasure; art should leave room for the imagination and the reasoning faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-describing or over-reproducing unpleasant original details (smells, sounds, repulsive aspects); provide enough for identification but allow audience inference. Anti-pattern: literal labeling of pictures or excessive literalness that removes interpretive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure of identification and problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of aesthetic pleasure comes from the audience's pleasure in identifying the likeness or solving the 'puzzle' of representation; if the original is unknown, pleasure is due to execution (colouring, technique).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure works to invite recognition or cognitive engagement; excellence of execution compensates when the original is unfamiliar. Example: detective stories and puzzles exploit this pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry is innate and should be engaged
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of mimicry is innate in humans and enjoyment of mimicry is natural; art should engage this innate tendency to produce pleasure and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imitation and recognizable patterns to tap into intuitive public responses; early, simple mimicry can be developed into complex artistry. Anti-pattern: relying solely on abstract or opaque procedures that thwart instinctive mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and order are natural pleasures — use symmetry and cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm, harmony and order (symmetry, cadence) are natural sources of delight (children delight in rhythm); metre is a variant of rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ rhythmic regularities (meter, cadence) and symmetrical structures to tap basic aesthetic pleasures. Consider cultural/psychological universals but also test audience response. Anti-pattern: chaotic or formless rhythm when clarity of cadence is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama must represent social interaction (more than one person)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy (and drama) are fictitious realization of fully conscious life and must involve more than one person, since man is a social animal and dynamics arise from associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design dramatic scenes with interacting agents whose associations bring potentials into energeia; avoid isolating a drama into monologic exposition unless intentionally experimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot/Action (praxis) as the basis in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama’s basis is praxis (action); Homer’s merit for epic is different (epic’s praxis-basis differs), but drama needs action-realization as its foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose dramatic works driven by intentional actions and their consequences rather than merely by description or philosophical exposition. Scoring note: evaluate how tightly actions determine causal outcomes in the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of combined forms changes effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain forms (e.g. dithyrambic and nomic poetry, some tragedies) employ dance, tune and verse simultaneously, while others use them in separate parts; combination alters the audience effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether to combine musical/dance/verse elements to intensify or diversify the imaginative clothing; choose combinations intentionally for effect rather than by accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match artistic aim to form (ultimate aim names the work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Things are called after their ultimate aim; the aim (artistic vs scientific) determines whether a work is 'poetry' or something else — i.e. form should reflect purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing form and style, ensure that the medium and devices serve the ultimate artistic aim (evoking emotion, representing action, instructing). Anti-pattern: selecting a form (e.g. hexameter) for accidental reasons rather than because it serves the work’s aim.
